The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.

	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

content.text:
**Newsboat** and **podboat** are a pair of terminal (TUI) programs that ship together in the same package — think of them as the RSS-reading cousins of the newsraft you already have.

## Newsboat
A terminal RSS/Atom **feed reader**. It's the direct successor to the old Newsbeuter project and is one of the most popular TUI feed readers.

- Reads your subscriptions from a `~/.newsboat/urls` file (one feed URL per line, optional tags/titles).
- Config lives in `~/.newsboat/config` — heavily customizable: keybindings, colors, macros, "query feeds" (saved searches), and filters.
- Vim-ish navigation; can open articles in your browser, run macros, sync with services like Miniflux/FreshRSS/Nextcloud News/The Old Reader.
- Stores articles in a local SQLite cache so you can read offline.

## Podboat
A companion **podcast downloader** that comes bundled with newsboat (older name: "podbeuter").

- Podcasts are just RSS feeds where items carry an audio `<enclosure>`. In newsboat you mark an episode's enclosure for download; that queues it.
- You then launch `podboat`, which reads the download queue and fetches the actual audio files to disk.
- It's a download manager, **not** a player — it grabs the `.mp3`/`.m4a` files; you play them in whatever player you like.

## How this relates to your setup
- **newsraft** (what you have) is a newer, lighter alternative to newsboat — similar TUI, similar `feeds` file concept, but a separate project. Its equivalent of podboat is just marking enclosures for download within newsraft itself.
- Your current pipeline uses **luna-podcatcher** as the thing that fetches/transcribes podcasts and re-serves them as RSS on `localhost:19091`, with newsraft as the front-end. Newsboat+podboat would be an alternative stack: newsboat as reader, podboat as the downloader — no luna-podcatcher needed, but also no transcripts.

Both are in nixpkgs and Homebrew (single `newsboat` package provides both binaries) if you ever want to compare them against newsraft. Want me to note the differences or set one up to trial?

############ PAGER / LINKS / ATTACHMENTS (lines 70-100) ############
view item's content you have to go to _pager_ menu by entering selected item.

_Pager_ menu will display some details about selected item and render its
content if it was provided by feed. Usually feed item entries have a links
section with one link pointing to a related web page and several links that were
mentioned in the item's content. You can copy these links into your clipboard
with *y* key and open them in your web browser with *o* key. To target a key
action to link with a specific index you have to prefix your key with this
index. For example, *5y* will copy fifth link and *17o* will open seventeenth
link in the web browser. You can also setup custom command bindings to execute
any commands with these links. Consider this *config* file:

	_bind m exec mpv "%l"_++
_bind f exec feh "%l"_

With this you will be able to open any link in *mpv*(1) and *feh*(1) directly
from your terminal! Isn't it awesome? It is freaking amazing!

For both _sections_ menu and _feeds_ menu there is a special explore mode. You
can toggle it by pressing the *tab* key. It's truly miraculous: it reveals all
the news in the current context (combines news from all feeds of the current
menu into one list). This mode may come in handy when you want to quickly scroll
through all the news without switching between sections and feeds back and forth.

And for a dessert, I'll tell you about the search functionality. You can type
*/* to begin search input - enter the desired query here and press *Enter*. This
will open up an _items_ menu with all the items matching your query in the
current context.

# CONFIGURATION


############ EXEC action + format specifiers (lines 165,200 & specifier table) ############
in the *ACTIONS* section. Here's an example:

	*bind* r _reload-all_

The special _exec_ action makes it possible to run shell commands when the bound
key is pressed. Specifiers within the command are replaced with values
corresponding to the currently selected entry as per *menu-item-entry-format*:

	*bind* m _exec_ w3m "%l"

There's also *exec-quiet*, which does the same but doesn't update the UI.
Useful with commands which are guaranteed not to take over the terminal:

	*bind* m _exec-quiet_ setsid mpv --terminal=no "%l" &

The _edit_ action runs a specified SQL query on the *database*, so please be
careful! _@selected_ specifier is replaced with a condition which identifies the
currently selected entry - make sure to include it if you want to target
individual item/feed rather than the whole database:

	*bind* w _edit_ UPDATE items SET user_data = json_set(IFNULL(user_data, '{}'), '$.toWatch', 1) WHERE _@selected_++
*bind* W _edit_ UPDATE items SET user_data = json_set(IFNULL(user_data, '{}'), '$.toWatch', 0) WHERE _@selected_

Use the _find_ action to retrieve items based on a specified SQL condition in
the current context. For instance, to search for items marked as toWatch (as
shown in the previous example), one can use the bindings like the following:

	*bind* f _find_ user_data LIKE '%"toWatch":1%'++
*bind* f _find_ json_extract(user_data, '$.toWatch') = 1

Binding lines can fit multiple actions in a single key. These actions will be
executed in the order in which they are specified. Assigned actions
must be separated with semicolon (;) characters, for example:

	*bind* key _action_; _exec_ command; _action_; _edit_ query; _action_

In case you want to disable some binding which was set in Newsraft by default,
you can use a line according to this format:

	*unbind* key

content.text:
Short answer: **not with a built-in download queue like podboat — but yes, you can absolutely do it via a key binding.** Newsraft has no dedicated "podcast download manager." Instead it exposes each item's **links list** in the pager (which includes the audio *attachment*/enclosure URL), and lets you bind any key to run a shell command on the selected link. So you wire up your own downloader.

## How it works

Every feed item's audio enclosure is stored as an **attachment** (URL + MIME type + size) and shows up in the item's **links list** in the pager. You target a specific link by **prefixing its index**, then trigger a binding. The magic specifier is `%l` = the selected link's URL (`exec`/`exec-quiet` run a shell command with it substituted in).

The upstream example config only shows *streaming* (mpv), but the same mechanism downloads:

```
bind m exec mpv --no-terminal "%l" &        # stream the selected link in mpv
```

## Config to actually download

Your `~/.config/newsraft/config` is currently empty. Add something like:

```sh
# Download the selected link (e.g. a podcast enclosure) into ~/Podcasts
bind d exec-quiet sh -c 'mkdir -p ~/Podcasts && curl -L --output-dir ~/Podcasts -O "%l"' &

# Or, nicer filenames/metadata for podcasts:
bind D exec-quiet sh -c 'yt-dlp -P ~/Podcasts "%l"' &

# Stream instead of download:
bind m exec mpv --no-terminal "%l" &
```

**Usage:** open a podcast item → in the pager you'll see the numbered links list → find the index of the audio enclosure (e.g. it's link `3`) → type `3d` to download it (or `3m` to stream). Without an index prefix it acts on the first/related link.

## Notes for your setup
- Your podcast items come **through luna-podcatcher** (`localhost:19091`), so the enclosure URL each item exposes is whatever luna serves (e.g. the original `media.transistor.fm/...mp3`). That's what gets downloaded — newsraft just runs curl on it.
- This is **cross-platform** — same config works on macOS (ties back to your earlier question; there newsraft's default open command is `open "%l"`).
- If you'd rather have a true fire-and-forget **download queue** (mark episodes, batch-download later), that's exactly what **newsboat + podboat** give out of the box — newsraft's model is one-off `exec` bindings instead.

Fully reconciled now. Here's the complete picture.

## Why the build failed

The `ollama-cuda` **CUDA sub-build fails at CMake configure** because CMake can't locate `nvcc`:

```
-- Could not find `nvcc` executable in path specified by environment variable
   CUDAToolkit_ROOT=/nix/store/…libcublas-dev/…cuda_cudart/…libcublas-include/…cuda_cccl/…libcublas-lib
CMake Error at …/ggml-cuda/CMakeLists.txt:268 (message): CUDA Toolkit not found
```

Everything else (all the CPU backends) builds fine — only the CUDA target dies, which fails the whole derivation.

The subtlety: `cuda_nvcc-12.9.86` **is** in the derivation's build closure — nvcc is *there*. The bug is that the derivation hands CMake a malformed `CUDAToolkit_ROOT` — a run-together concatenation of the cuBLAS/cudart/cccl output paths that **omits the nvcc output**. CMake's `FindCUDAToolkit` treats that variable as a single root and looks for `bin/nvcc` under it, doesn't find it, and errors. So this is a **CUDA-packaging bug in this nixpkgs revision**, not a missing dependency and not your `hosts/lucie/default.nix` config (`package = pkgs.ollama-cuda;` is fine).

## What introduced it

It's the **uncommitted `flake.lock` bump**. Your working-tree lock moved top-level nixpkgs:

- committed: `421eebfd` → working: **`335f0738` (2026-07-24)** — matches the failing system name `…lucie-26.11.20260724.335f073`.

That bump pulled in `ollama-cuda 0.32.1` from a nixpkgs revision where the CUDA build is broken. Your committed lock (before the bump) is the last state that presumably built.

## Fix options

| Option | Command / change | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Revert the bump** (recommended) | `git checkout -- flake.lock` | Returns to the last-good lock; discards the *entire* bump (all inputs), so you'd re-bump later once the CUDA fix lands upstream. Keeps a recent ollama. |
| **2. Pin ollama to stable** | `package = stablePkgs.ollama-cuda;` in `hosts/lucie/default.nix:139` | Surgical, keeps the bump — but stable is **0.21.1** vs 0.32.1. That's a big downgrade and may not run your `gemma4:26b` well. Not great for your setup. |
| **3. Forward-update just nixpkgs** | `nix flake update nixpkgs` | Only helps if a *newer* revision already fixed the CUDA path bug — speculative, could still be broken. |

Given you're serving `gemma4:26b`, I'd avoid the 0.21.1 downgrade. **Option 1** is the clean move: the bump isn't committed, so reverting loses nothing permanent (you can regenerate it later with `nix flake update`).
